title: What was the deadliest war in history?
subtitle: The Taiping Rebellion
subject: histoire
description: Most people think of World War II. Yet depending on how you count the dead, the deadliest conflict in history is a 19th-century Chinese civil war, born from the visions of a failed candidate in the imperial examinations.
author: vedran-obucina

hero.hook: Twenty to thirty million dead, led by a man who called himself the younger brother of Jesus: the deadliest war in history is not the one you think.

blocks.text: The deadliest war in history? Many people answer at once: World War II. But it all depends on how you count. Some historians count only those who died in battle. Others add the civilians carried off by the famine and disease that war drags behind it.

By that second method, the leading candidate is the Taiping Rebellion, the huge uprising that shook China between **1850 and 1864**. Conservative estimates speak of **20 to 30 million** dead, others go higher, and the exact figure will never be known. Most surprising of all, it began as a religious movement. How did a new faith set off a war on such a scale?

sections.title: Hong Xiuquan, younger brother of Jesus

blocks.text: [[Hong Xiuquan]] was a failed candidate in the [[imperial examinations]], the famous competitive exams that opened the doors of the Chinese civil service. These exams rested on [[Confucianism]], one of China's three great traditions of thought alongside Daoism and Buddhism. After reading some Christian texts, Hong reread his own visions and dreams in their light.

blocks.caption: Hong Xiuquan, the "Heavenly King," in a 19th-century engraving.

blocks.text: His conclusion was dizzying: God was his heavenly father, Jesus his older brother, and he himself the younger brother of Jesus. This belief gave him a religious authority of his own: God had charged him with removing evil and establishing a new kingdom on Earth. His followers founded the [[Taiping Heavenly Kingdom]], a self-styled state in southern China with its own doctrines and its own rites, far removed from classical Christianity. And with the new religion grew political power.

The Taiping did not simply copy European Christianity. Their religion combined Protestant ideas with Chinese traditions, and claimed that the high God, Shangdi, had chosen Hong Xiuquan to establish a heavenly kingdom on Earth.

The Taiping wanted to crush the [[Qing dynasty]], the imperial power that ruled China. But they were not mere power-seekers: they were zealots. They believed they were carrying out God's command and building a just kingdom under his authority. Their armies quickly conquered vast areas of southern China.

The movement gave itself an administration, laws, a hierarchy, an army and officials. Hong proclaimed himself Heavenly King, a very Chinese title and not a Christian one at all, resting on the claim that God himself had chosen him. The Qing went to war against the rebels, but this clash of armies soon became a religious conflict: who had the right to rule in God's name?

The Taiping tried to ban opium smoking, footbinding, arranged marriage and the worship of traditional religious images. More than a change of rulers, these reforms aimed at a complete rebuilding of society.

The Taiping's first great success came in **1853**, when they seized [[Nanjing]], one of China's most important cities. They renamed it Tianjing, the "Heavenly Capital." The message was clear: God supported the rebellion, and the new kingdom would spread according to his plan. The Taiping armies then pushed north and west. Their Northern March came close to Beijing, the Qing capital, but failed.

blocks.caption: The Ming walls of Nanjing, which the Taiping held for eleven years.

blocks.text: In the lower Yangtze basin, the fighting turned to horror. The siege of [[Anqing]], retaken by the Qing in **1861**, was especially gruesome, and the fall of the city opened the road to Nanjing. The countryside was devastated: farming destroyed, epidemics, famine. Yet the Taiping soldiers kept praying before every battle, listening to sermons and believing firmly in their mission.

Nanjing withstood nearly two years of siege. The Taiping fighters fiercely defended what they held to be God's Kingdom. But the Qing cut off supplies. In **July 1864**, their troops entered the city and took it. Hong had died shortly before, and the Heavenly Kingdom fell apart.

blocks.caption: The recapture of Nanjing by imperial troops in July 1864, in a Qing court painting.

blocks.text: Claiming to be the younger brother of Jesus gave these fighters a clear authority and a goal larger than worldly power. The Qing were not a simple opponent in a civil war: they embodied an evil rule that had to be destroyed. Such religious extremism leaves no room for compromise. Either it wins and imposes its order, or everyone dies.

events.detail: In July, imperial troops enter the city.

blocks.text: A war of religion, a civil war and a power struggle all at once, the Taiping Rebellion killed 20 to 30 million people: without its theology, neither its birth nor its fanaticism can be understood.
